kresling_choice.reason: the smallest barrier strain that is still positive among the options with 2n star points fine enough for the radial deployment (perimeter kept by 16 pleats)

opening.rule: centred on the axis of the folded body sliding on the chute; radius = tail neck at full size plus 12 mm; vertical face 15 mm ahead of the arm envelope

bore.rule: arm passage radius 110 mm plus the rack slots and the cradle on the collar inside the bore circle; bottom 17 mm above the waterline

womb.floor_reason: floating alone, the floor in the water gives the wide waterplane the chamber needs for roll stability

tail.reason: seam section from the bore and the magnet ring; top line the steepest that clears the folded arm and the parts; flat bottom over the low aft parts; rounded aft cap

checks.text: Docked with 11.9 L of gel in the trough and the arm folded, gel chamber and tail float as one egg at z -149 mm, level with 5.0 L in the trim tank, roll GM 85 mm.

Trim stays within 0.05 deg while the gel moves from the tail into the trough and within 0.00 deg after (printing -0.00, newborn at the lip -0.00, after the birth -0.00; positive is stern down); the tail pump moves water in the trim tank (5.0 L folded, 10.1 L printing, 13.0 L at the lip, 14 L tank).
The birth opening stays above the water: the lowest point of the opening is 42 mm or more above the waterline in every state.

Docking height: the gel chamber takes 6.8 L of water into two ballast bags beside the trough and floats at z -145 mm like the tail (z -145 mm); the faces meet within the 23 mm the cone captures (gel chamber trim 0.4 deg). The bags let out as much water as gel comes in, so the egg keeps the docking height.
Before docking the bottom of the docking bore is 23 mm above water on the gel chamber and 20 mm on the tail.
Docked, the bottom of the bore sits 24 mm above the waterline, inside the dock seal.

Gel trough (the sketch of 21 Nov): 265 x 180 mm inside, floor at z -305 mm, gel surface at z -155 mm, so the gel covers the folded print by 15 mm and leaves 15 mm under the belly. 11.9 L of gel, against 11.9 L to fill the gel chamber bottom to the same level and 24.1 L at the least; the rest of the gel chamber stays air. The flat floor hangs up to 141 mm under the curved hull, a shallow keel.

Gel supply: carrying the 11.9 L in the tail would sink the tail about 45 mm and put the bore under water before docking, so the tail keeps a 1 L buffer and the gel pump, the buffer is topped up through the dock line from a shore tank, and the gel goes through the bottom channel into the floor of the trough: 2.0 L/min through 0.9 m of 12 mm line needs 29 kPa against the 100 kPa of the pump class (Bingham flow, plastic viscosity 0.3 Pa s, an estimate); the trough fills from below in 5.9 min, level by itself.
The gel surface (z -155 mm) is 30 mm under the bottom of the docking bore.

The kit stays where the arm sets the kit: the kit is lighter than the gel, and 2.5 Pa of yield stress is enough to stop the kit rising (the gel has 25 Pa); the three saddle feet sit in three cups on the seat.

Docking ring, thin: a 4 mm PETG lip flush with the shell on each face, plus three 44 x 44 mm bosses 6 mm thick behind the 40 x 40 x 4 mm steel pads of the FluxGrip FG40 magnets. At the worst dock load of 72 N per magnet (v2 design) a boss bends to 5 MPa, and at the full 250 N rating to 19 MPa, against about 50 MPa for PETG.

Birth opening rim, thin: a 3 mm PETG lip rolled into the 3 mm shell, no magnets. The rim only carries the friction of the body sliding out (under 4 N) and keeps the D 200 opening round; the front plate already carries the shell loads.

Arm out of the tail: the boom slides the folded DexArm (passage pose, stem turned forward) through the bore; the arm stays inside R 175 mm of the R 200 mm bore, closest 11.1 mm to any part (tail shell).
Reach over the whole print: all 59888 G-code points reached within 0.000 mm inside the official joint ranges (base -15 to 18, J1 31 to 88, J2 75 to 79 deg), boom A from -325 to -79 mm.

Collisions while printing: every link and the tool stay 17.3 mm or more from the shell, the trough walls, the walls, chute and cradle (closest: tool head to the chute; the needle in the work is left out).
Only the stem enters the gel: the lowest link is 40 mm and the tool head 16 mm above the gel surface.
After the kit is set, the stem misses every kit part; closest pass 3.4 mm.
Kit pick and place with the suction module: reached within 0.00 mm, closest 3.1 mm (tool to the rack forks); module and kit, or module and the worst gel load, 320 g, under the 500 g payload.

Suction hold: a 15 mm cup at 35 kPa holds 6.19 N in theory and 3.71 N at a 60 % seal on the flat silicone face of the saddle (46 x 50 mm). Loads on the cup: 1.11 N carrying in air; -0.94 N while lowering through the gel (the gel pushes the kit into the cup: 0.87 N of yield bearing and side shear against 1.05 N of weight less 1.12 N of buoyancy); 0.81 N if the kit had to be lifted back out of the gel. Safety factor 3.3 on the worst case. A sideways move in the gel would load the cup with 0.54 N in shear and peel, so the path only moves the kit sideways in air.
Tool change 1 (needle module to suction module) at the rack on the docking wall, boom at x -510 mm: reached within 0.00 mm, closest 2.6 mm (tool to the rack forks, up, clear of the rack); 39 s.

Tool change 2 (suction module to needle module) at the rack on the docking wall, boom at x -510 mm: reached within 0.00 mm, closest 2.6 mm (tool to the rack forks, the cup module comes beside the slot); 48 s.

Module mount: the Rotrics quick release (press the end effector button, pull the module off; push the next one on until the latch clicks; 5 pin module port). A pin on each fork presses the button as the module settles, so the change needs no extra motor. Rotrics asks for the arm to be off during a change; a powered change through the rack needs a bench test, otherwise the tail switches the arm off for the 1.5 s of the release, with the arm resting on the brakes in that pose (both untested).

Reach and clearance along the push: reached within 0.00 mm, closest 16.2 mm (EE to the stern plate). The septum and push boss sit 20 mm below the axis on the tail cap, so the arm pushes lower and the forearm keeps clear of the shell under the opening.
When the arm lets go, the needle tip is 107 mm from the rim of the opening.

Push while inflating: while the arm pushes, no segment opens inside the gel chamber. The air is metered by the push position (12 L/min pump), so each of the 8 segments opens only after the segment has passed out through the stern opening, front first; the push waits for the air. Only while the arm holds at full reach do the last segments at the narrow tail end open at the rim (full radius at the first rings up to 88 mm, against the 100 mm rim).
The folded part passes the D 200 opening: the body slides over the lip, where the chute runs flush into the rim, and keeps 47 mm to the rest of the rim (folded diameter 120 mm).

Arm force within the DexArm payload: peak 4.19 N against 4.91 N (500 g). Before the first segment is out the folded body (0.77 kg after the gel is drained) climbs the chute on the arm alone: 4.19 N at friction 0.2; once a segment opens outside, the pressure on the rim pulls the body out (up to 11.3 N) and the arm force falls.

Margin on friction: the chute is lined with PTFE film and wet with gel (friction 0.2 assumed, bench test needed), and the trapped gel is drained first, so the whole folded body (0.77 kg) on the steepest part of the chute (19 deg) needs 3.92 N at friction 0.2 and 4.63 N at 0.3, within the 4.91 N payload; 5.34 N at 0.4 and 6.75 N at 0.6 would not be (bare PETG).

Drain before the climb: air through the needle at 450 Pa pushes the trapped gel out of a 6 mm duckbill vent in the nose: 238 Pa shears the gel plug inside the folded body, 212 Pa drives 0.31 L/min through the vent, 0.70 L out in 2.3 min, 0.12 L left in the fold corners (estimate). The gel round the body keeps the folds shut: opening a fold inside the gel needs about 600 Pa. The body goes from 1.47 to 0.77 kg.
Stem bending at the peak push: 12G needle 127 MPa, 6 x 4 mm tube 34 MPa, against about 200 MPa yield for 304 stainless.

All the air goes in through the arm: a pump in the tail feeds an air line along the boom and the arm to the 12G needle in the valve on the tail cap; 12 L/min needs about 4.8 kPa, well within a 20 kPa diaphragm pump. No other source fills the body.

The needle stays in the valve until the body is full: the arm pushes until the tail end reaches x 265 mm, the farthest it reaches with the needle boss 20 mm low and 10 mm to the shell, then holds there from 304 s while the rest of the air goes in (the segments still inside are at the narrow tail end and pass the rim as they open); full at 401 s, then the needle comes out and the arm lets go. While holding, the opened part pulls the needle outward with at most 10.07 N, against a few newtons of grip of a 12G needle in a silicone septum (estimate, bench test).

The sketch path (inflate to full size inside the gel chamber, then leave through the high opening) does not work: the full body is 376 mm across against the 200 mm opening, and in air the 1.47 kg body would have to be lifted 199 mm, while the DexArm payload is 0.5 kg. The birth therefore keeps the push while inflating: folded inside, opening segment by segment outside.

Telescopic boom at full reach: 488 mm beyond the rail end; the second stage is an 80 x 16 mm aluminum box tube with a 2 mm wall (3.4 times stiffer in bending than the old 120 x 6 mm plate, and lighter), tip deflection under the arm and push 0.9 mm; the tube corner passes the bore at radius 185 of 200 mm.
Dock: the tail arrives at 19 mm/s on two small pumps; the cone centers the collar and the three FluxGrip magnets switch on after contact and hold 750 N.

Full size newborn: 0.53 m long and 0.37 m across, 35 L (the gel chamber inside is 0.75 m long, 0.70 wide, 0.58 tall: 70 % of the length, 54 % of the width). Limited by the skin area that packs into the printed 0.20 x 0.12 m envelope and by a stable 25 percent stretch.

The newborn floats upright: 0.77 kg dry would float 32 mm deep, so the kit pumps take 0.9 L of water into a belly pocket; then 50 mm deep with the kit pumps 50 mm under water, centre of gravity 118 mm under the axis.
The newborn swims on the two kit jets at 0.12 m/s.

Small pumps (DFRobot FIT0800, 100 L/h, 4 mm jet, 0.026 N each): the docked egg swims at 0.11 m/s on four and turns at 1.3 deg/s on one; the gel chamber alone swims at 0.07 m/s and turns at 4.1 deg/s. Slow, as accepted.
